<details>
The PKGBUILD defines sources that are fetched from the project's official GitHub repository (https://github.com/nearai/ironclaw), using predictable URLs tied to a specific tag (`${_pkgname}-v${pkgver}`). The `source` array retrieves shell completion scripts via the `raw/refs/tags` path, and the binary tarballs are downloaded from the official GitHub releases page. All checksums are provided and non-SKIP, which enhances integrity, though even if they were SKIP, that would not make this stage unsafe.

The PKGBUILD does not contain any top-level command substitutions, `pkgver()` function overrides, or immediate execution of downloaded content during sourcing. The `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` command will only fetch and extract the sources, and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` only reads metadata — neither will execute the `package()` function or any build steps. There are no uses of `curl`, `wget`, `eval`, `base64`, or other dangerous constructs at global scope or in `pkgver()`. The file adheres to standard AUR packaging practices and poses no risk during the specified commands.
</details>
<evidence>

No dangerous code executes during source fetch and parse</summary>
</security_assessment>

There is no use of `curl`, `wget`, `eval`, `base64`, or other potentially dangerous constructs that could indicate code injection or dynamic payload retrieval.

All file installations are performed on local files extracted or copied into `$srcdir`, with proper permissions set during packaging. No network operations, runtime modifications, or suspicious commands occur during the `package()` function.

While the sources include raw scripts fetched via `raw/refs/tags/`, these are shell completion files — not executable installers — and their integrity is protected by matching SHA-256 checksums. The use of GitHub's raw content URLs is common in AUR packages when upstream does not provide tarballs of auxiliary files. Given the presence of verified hashes and no evidence of dynamic code execution or data exfiltration, this package poses no supply-chain risk.
